title: Modern amphibians begin to diversify

facts.text: Lissamphibians, the modern amphibians, began to diversify in the Jurassic, including the first modern frogs and salamanders.
The stem-caecilian Eocaecilia is known from the Early Jurassic of Arizona; stem-frogs and albanerpetontids follow in the Middle Jurassic.
Of the once-diverse temnospondyls, only brachyopoids survived into the Jurassic.

title: Pangean megamonsoon breaks down

facts.text: At the start of the Jurassic the Pangean megamonsoon began to fall apart as Gondwana and southern Laurasia dried out.
The monsoon kept weakening through the Jurassic as the continents drifted apart.
The Pangean megamonsoon is the hypothesis that Pangaea had a distinct seasonal reversal of winds, causing extreme transitions between dry and wet periods through the year.

The megamonsoon would have led to immensely arid regions with extremely hot days and frigid nights in the interior of the supercontinent, making those areas nearly uninhabitable to terrestrial ecosystems.
When Pangaea finally broke apart by the middle Mesozoic, the megamonsoon fell apart completely.

title: Plesiosaurs diversify in the earliest Jurassic

facts.text: A rich radiation of plesiosaurs is known from the Hettangian, implying the group had already diversified in the Late Triassic.
Most plesiosaurs in the Hettangian Blue Lias were short-necked rhomaleosaurids.
Large plesiosaurs joined sharks and other ichthyosaurs as predators of ichthyosaurs.
Plesiosaurs also invaded fresh water; small forms are known from Jurassic China and Australia.
By the Toarcian, about 180 million years ago, longer-necked plesiosaurids reached up to 10 metres.

facts.text: In China's Sichuan Basin, hot, arid fernlands of the Triassic–Jurassic transition gave way to cheirolepid conifer floras in the Hettangian and Sinemurian.
Ferns and other plants with dissected leaves coped better with the crisis and spread across the boundary into the Jurassic.
The extinct conifer family Cheirolepidiaceae, known by its Classopollis pollen, was abundant through the Jurassic.

title: Marine life recovers from the end-Triassic extinction

facts.text: In Britain, seafloor communities began recovering almost at once after the extinction, despite repeated relapses into anoxia.
Oxygen depletion and nutrient runoff persisted into the Hettangian and may have delayed recovery.
In Argentina's Neuquén Basin, recovery ran from the late early Hettangian to a new balance of diversity by the late Hettangian.
The carbon cycle settled only in the Sinemurian, when brachiopods and dasycladacean algae rediversified.
Tropical reefs, which had collapsed, did not fully recover until much later in the Jurassic.

title: Ammonites radiate explosively

facts.text: Ammonoids, almost wiped out at the end of the Triassic, radiated into many new forms with complex sutures: the ammonites proper.
The orders Psiloceratina, Ammonitina, Lytoceratina, Haploceratina, Perisphinctina and Ancyloceratina all appeared during the Jurassic.
Jurassic ammonite faunas formed about 20 provinces in a northern Pan-Boreal and a southern Pan-Tethyan realm.
Serpenticone ammonites, coiled like snakes, are abundant in Europe's Jurassic rocks.

title: Archaic dinosaur lineages die out

facts.text: Basal neotheropods such as coelophysoids and dilophosaurs survived into the Early Jurassic but were gone by the Middle Jurassic.
Bipedal basal sauropodomorphs such as the massospondylids also died out by the start of the Middle Jurassic.

title: Crocodylomorphs radiate; thalattosuchians go to sea

facts.text: Crocodylomorphs radiated rapidly in the Early Jurassic, filling niches different from their Triassic relatives.
The mostly marine Thalattosuchia first appeared then and became a prominent part of marine ecosystems.
One of the oldest thalattosuchians, a basal teleosauroid from Morocco, dates from the Hettangian–Sinemurian.
A protosuchid from Arizona is the earliest known plant-eating crocodylomorph.

title: Dinosaurs become dominant land vertebrates

facts.text: With rival reptile groups gone after the end-Triassic extinction, dinosaurs surged in diversity and abundance in the Early Jurassic.
Land faunas shifted from joint rule by dinosauromorphs and pseudosuchians to dominance by dinosaurs alone.
From the Early Jurassic, dinosaurs and pterosaurs were the commonest land reptiles; lizards and tuatara relatives filled the small-reptile roles.
Dinosaurs had spread to every continent by the Early Jurassic at the latest.
They stayed the dominant land vertebrates through the Jurassic and Cretaceous, until 66 million years ago.

title: Earliest definitive ornithischians

facts.text: The earliest definitive ornithischian dinosaurs appeared and diversified in the Early Jurassic.
They included small basal forms such as Lesothosaurus, the heterodontosaurids and early thyreophorans.
Early ornithischians were relatively small, averaging about 1–2 meters in body length, and were bipedal.
The place of Heterodontosauridae is disputed: one view treats them as very early ornithischians like Lesothosaurus, while a 2021 study nested them alongside Pachycephalosauria.

title: Farallon plate subducts under North America

facts.text: The Farallon plate began sinking beneath western North America in the Early Jurassic, as Pangaea broke apart.
Mountains in Nevada and California kept rising as plate motions pushed North America northward.
During its subduction the Farallon plate accreted island arcs and terranes to the North American plate, and much of western North America is composed of these accreted terranes.
Most of the Farallon plate was subducted, but two remnants persist today: the Cocos plate under Central America and the Juan de Fuca plate under Washington, Oregon and northern California.

title: Last Dicroidium seed ferns

facts.text: Dicroidium, a seed fern that dominated Triassic Gondwanan floras, survived only as a relict in Antarctica into the Early Jurassic.
The related peltasperm Lepidopteris likewise lingered in Patagonia.
Dicroidium-dominated ecosystems in Gondwana collapsed during the end-Triassic mass extinction.
Dicroidium species grew as large trees and were widely distributed and dominant over Gondwana during the Triassic.

title: Modern sharks and rays radiate

facts.text: Neoselachians, the group of all living sharks and rays, radiated from the Early Jurassic.
Rays (batomorphs) first appear in the Early Jurassic; the oldest confirmed ray, Antiquaobatis, is from the Pliensbachian of Germany.
The oldest six-gilled and carpet sharks are from the Pliensbachian and Toarcian of Europe.
By the Late Jurassic they had largely replaced hybodonts, the Triassic's dominant sharks, in the sea.
Timelines of Earth and of life date the first rays, along with glycymeridid bivalves, to about 165 Ma.

title: Oceans shift from aragonite to calcite seas

facts.text: During the Early Jurassic the world's oceans changed from aragonite-sea to calcite-sea chemistry.
The change favoured dissolving aragonite and precipitating calcite.
A fall in the Mg/Ca ratio of seawater favors the precipitation of calcite over aragonite.
Calcite sea conditions bring rapid, widespread formation of carbonate hardgrounds, calcitic ooids and calcite cements, and dissolution of aragonite shells in shallow warm seas.

title: Paleo-Tethys closes as Cimmeria collides

facts.text: In the Early Jurassic, Paleo-Tethys ocean floor subducted beneath the Cimmerian plate, closing the ocean from west to east.
The closure was part of the Cimmerian orogeny.
The Tethyan Trench formed around 200 million years ago as the Cimmerian plate subducted beneath eastern Laurasia.

facts.text: From the Early Jurassic, a seaway several hundred kilometres wide between the Baltic Shield and Greenland linked the Boreal Ocean to the proto-Atlantic.

facts.text: Coccolithophores and dinoflagellates, both first seen in the Triassic, radiated in the Early to Middle Jurassic and became prominent phytoplankton.
Coccolithophores have been an integral part of marine plankton since the Jurassic.
The rise of calcareous plankton in the Middle Jurassic altered ocean chemistry; their seafloor deposits buffered against large CO2 emissions.
Calcareous nannoplankton diversity kept growing through the Jurassic and Cretaceous.

title: Blue Lias limestones and shales deposited

facts.text: The Blue Lias, alternating limestone and shale beds, was laid down from the latest Triassic into the early Sinemurian.
Its rhythmic layers record short climate swings driven by orbital (Milankovitch) cycles.
It is rich in fossils; most of its Hettangian plesiosaurs are rhomaleosaurids.

facts.text: The Andean orogeny, still ongoing and responsible for raising the Andes, began in the Early Jurassic, about 200 million years ago.
Subduction-related volcanism along western South America has continued since about 200 million years ago.
Its first phases brought extension, rifting, back-arc basins and the emplacement of large batholiths.
Early subduction built the La Negra volcanic arc in northern Chile.
The Atacama Fault is thought to have formed as the orogeny began.

conflicts.note: Sollipulli and Taapaca (18958197adc7) pages date Andean subduction and volcanism from 185 Ma

facts.text: Conodonts, jawless fish whose tooth-like elements are key index fossils, finally died out at the start of the Jurassic, around 200 million years ago.
They had lasted more than 300 million years, since the Cambrian.
They vanished first in the Tethys and eastern Panthalassa; survivors lasted into the earliest Hettangian of Hungary and central Panthalassa.
By the end of the Triassic only a handful of conodont species remained.
A mid-Norian marine crisis, possibly linked to the Manicouagan impact, may have hastened their decline.

title: Navajo sand sea covers western North America

facts.text: In the Jurassic the Colorado Plateau grew ever drier until some 388,000 km² of western North America became a vast desert like the Sahara.
The Navajo Sandstone formed in an arid erg on western Pangaea, swept by winter monsoon winds; a 2019 radioisotopic study puts its start around 200–195 Ma.
Its dunes reached 670 m thick at Zion Canyon, where it now forms towering cliffs.

title: Pangaea splits into Laurasia and Gondwana

facts.text: Pangaea, which held all the major landmasses, began to rift apart around 200 million years ago; the breakup ran to about 160 million years ago.
Through the Early Jurassic it split into Laurasia (Eurasia and North America) in the north and Gondwana in the south; it had fully broken up by the Middle Jurassic.
By about 200 Ma the Central Pangean Mountains had worn down to a few uplands; widespread magmatism, including the Karoo and Ferrar provinces, preceded the rupture.
The breakup opened the Tethys between the landmasses and greatly strengthened the water cycle; another source has the Tethys Seaway splitting Pangaea in two only in the Late Jurassic.
North and South America separated in the Late Jurassic; by about 150 Ma their divergence was making oceanic crust off Colombia's Pacific coast.

facts.text: The Central American Seaway formed between about 200 and 154 million years ago, during the initial breakup of Pangaea.
North and South America, still joined when the Jurassic began, had rifted apart by the start of the Late Jurassic.
The seaway, also called the Hispanic Corridor, linked the North Atlantic and Tethys with eastern Panthalassa.
Fossil evidence suggests it was already open in the Early Jurassic; it closed only when the Isthmus of Panama formed.

title: First sauropods (Vulcanodon)

facts.text: Gravisaurian sauropods first appeared in the Early Jurassic; the oldest definite one, Vulcanodon of Zimbabwe, is likely Sinemurian.
Even earlier, the four-legged Ledumahadi of South Africa reached about 12 tonnes, far above other early sauropodomorphs.
By the end of the Early Jurassic, possibly after a global warming event, sauropods had become the dominant large plant-eaters on land.

events.date_text: during the Sinemurian, 200–193 million years ago (199.5–192.9 Ma)

date_display: during the Sinemurian, 200–193 million years ago (199.5–192.9 Ma)

facts.text: Sea level stayed near today's level in the Hettangian and Sinemurian, then rose several tens of metres in the late Sinemurian–Pliensbachian.
It fell back to near present levels by the late Pliensbachian.
During the latest part of the Toarcian the sea level again dropped by several tens of metres.
The earliest averostran theropods appeared in the Early Jurassic.
The oldest known ceratosaur, Saltriovenator, comes from the early Sinemurian of Italy, 199.3–197.5 million years ago.
Ceratosauria originally included the Coelophysoidea and Dilophosauridae as well, which implied a much earlier divergence of ceratosaurs from other theropods.

Abelisauroids flourished in the Southern Hemisphere in the Cretaceous, but their origins go back to at least the Middle Jurassic, with the earliest remains from Australian and South American deposits dated to about 170 million years ago.
The first part of the Jurassic was a cool interval lasting from about 199 to 183 million years ago.
Evidence suggests the late Pliensbachian was an icehouse, perhaps with Northern Hemisphere glaciation early and late in the stage.
Dropstones and glendonites in northeastern Siberia point to cold winters in the Early to Middle Jurassic.
It ended with a 4–8 °C warming spike in the early Toarcian.
The Charmouth Mudstone at Lyme Regis and Charmouth, England, yields complete skeletons of the armoured dinosaur Scelidosaurus, plus plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs.
It also holds large numbers of exceptional fish and a diverse insect fauna.
The Charmouth Mudstone Formation dates to the Early Jurassic (Sinemurian–Pliensbachian).
It is best exposed in the cliffs between Lyme Regis and Charmouth but extends north to Market Weighton in Yorkshire and underground in the East Midlands Shelf and Wessex Basin.
Argon–argon dating places an impact in today's Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, western Russia, at 195.9 ± 1.0 million years ago, in the Sinemurian.
The buried crater is 40 km across rim to rim and about 80 km including its ring terrace.
It is one of the major impact structures of the Jurassic.

title: First true crabs

facts.text: The first true crabs date from the Early Jurassic; the earliest, Eocarcinus praecursor of England, is early Pliensbachian.
Eocarcinus still lacked the crab-like body shape of modern crabs.
Shrimp and crabs both appear in the Jurassic.

facts.text: Volcanism in central Skåne, southern Sweden, had its first and main phase from the late Sinemurian to the Toarcian, about 191 to 178 million years ago.
A lahar at Korsaröd buried Early Jurassic wood, pollen and spores, preserving them exceptionally well.
The volcanism was a field of cinder cones with Strombolian eruption styles.
It was linked to the break-up of Pangea, and so is analogous to the much more voluminous Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts of Southern Africa.
Pliosaurs, short-necked plesiosaurs, evolved and entered the fossil record about 190 million years ago.
Many groups of primitive sea invertebrates appeared about the same time, and sponge reefs developed extensively.
Thalassophonea, the best-known pliosaur subclade, had crocodile-like short-necked forms with large heads and massive toothed jaws.
Pliosaurs range from 4 to 10 meters or more in length.
Around 190 million years ago the Pacific plate originated as a microplate at the triple junction of the Farallon, Phoenix and Izanagi plates.
A kink in one plate boundary turned the stable junction into an unstable one ringed by transform faults, creating the new plate at its centre.
It formed far from the margins of the Paleo-Pacific Ocean, in central Panthalassa.
A small impact made the 2.5 km Viewfield crater in Saskatchewan, Canada, about 190 ± 20 million years ago, in the Late Triassic or Early Jurassic.

title: Dilophosaurus, an early large predatory dinosaur

facts.text: Dilophosaurus, a theropod with a pair of thin arched skull crests, lived in North America about 186 million years ago.
About 7 m long and 400 kg, it was one of the earliest large predatory dinosaurs and the largest known land animal in North America at the time.
Known from Arizona's Kayenta Formation, it is cast as a top predator of its day, and Eubrontes footprints are widely credited to a theropod like it.

title: Earliest eutriconodont mammals

facts.text: The earliest eutriconodonts date from the Toarcian and already include several groups, such as Argentoconodon.
They later lived across Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas during the Jurassic and Cretaceous.

facts.text: The Toarcian extinction, about 183 million years ago, struck in two pulses: the Pliensbachian–Toarcian boundary event and the larger anoxic-event pulse.
It was catastrophic for corals: 90.9% of Tethyan coral species and 49% of genera were wiped out.
Ammonoids, already squeezed by the Gibbosus Event a million years earlier, suffered further losses.
On land, seed ferns and spore plants declined, possibly from mercury poisoning.
Megalosaurid dinosaurs diversified later in the Toarcian, perhaps filling niches emptied by the die-off.

facts.text: The Karoo and Ferrar provinces of southern Africa and Antarctica erupted about 183 million years ago, just before Gondwana's breakup.
With about 2.5 million cubic kilometres of magma, it is one of Earth's most extensive large igneous provinces.
As southern Africa passed over the Bouvet hotspot, basalt flooded the Clarens desert and covered nearly all of southern Africa.
Magmatism spread to Namibia, Lesotho, Lebombo and Antarctica by 184–175 Ma; Patagonia's Chon Aike province peaked 183–173 Ma.
Its timing matches the Toarcian anoxic event and the Pliensbachian–Toarcian extinction.

facts.text: The Posidonia Shale at Holzmaden, Germany, laid down about 183 million years ago during the anoxic event, holds superb complete fish and marine reptile skeletons.
Its stagnant-basin preservation became a benchmark for other fossil sites.
A 182.7-million-year-old ichthyosaur from it still contained collagen and blood cells; a plesiosaur kept traces of skin.
About 183 million years ago, early in the Toarcian, oxygen vanished from wide areas of the ocean; it is the only oceanic anoxic event documented from the Jurassic.
It was possibly the most extreme case of widespread ocean deoxygenation in the entire Phanerozoic.
Karoo-Ferrar CO2 warmed the climate, acidified the oceans and boosted weathering; the nutrient flood eutrophied the seas and drove anoxia.
The carbon release was large enough to disrupt the otherwise steady 9-million-year carbon cycle of the Jurassic.
Toarcian anoxia laid down organic-rich black shales, including oil shales mined commercially in China.
Global temperatures spiked by about 4–8 °C early in the Toarcian; the warm interval lasted until about 174 million years ago.
Sea surface temperatures likely topped 30 °C, and Pangaea's interior probably exceeded 40 °C.
The rapid warming intensified tropical storms worldwide, and a stronger water cycle made lakes expand.
A brief cold snap interrupted the warming just before the anoxic event.
Sea level rose gradually to a peak of about 75 metres above today's during the Toarcian.
Rifting between North America and Africa came first, beginning in the Early Jurassic, with rift basins such as the Newark Basin from Mexico to Nova Scotia.
The central Atlantic ocean basin began opening about 180 million years ago as a narrow ocean between the northern and southern parts of Pangaea.
Seafloor spreading between North America and Africa–South America began the breakup of Pangaea.
The North Atlantic stayed narrow through the Jurassic; the South Atlantic did not open until the Cretaceous.
The oldest large-scale ocean crust still surviving, in the northwest Atlantic and west Pacific, is about 180–200 million years old.

facts.text: Gondwana started to fragment around 180 million years ago, after the fast emplacement of the Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts.
Madagascar and Antarctica began rifting away from Africa, opening the western Indian Ocean.
The oldest magnetic anomalies show initial break-up in today's southern Weddell Sea about 180 to 160 million years ago.
Rifting at Falkland latitudes began about 190 million years ago, pushing Patagonia westward.
Fragmentation sped up in the Cretaceous and was largely complete by its end.

title: Marine reptile turnover at the Early–Middle Jurassic boundary

facts.text: Between the end of the Toarcian and the start of the Bajocian, most ichthyosaur lineages appear to have died out.
Ophthalmosaurids appeared in the early Bajocian and from then on made up almost all ichthyosaurs.
Among plesiosaurs, microcleidids died out and rhomaleosaurids nearly so, while cryptoclidids, the dominant later Jurassic group, appeared in the Bajocian.

title: First Ginkgo

facts.text: The earliest members of the genus Ginkgo, with ovule and pollen organs like the living species, appear in the Middle Jurassic of the Northern Hemisphere.
Ginkgoales were among the most important parts of Eurasian Jurassic floras.
Ginkgo is represented today by a single species, Ginkgo biloba.
Other Jurassic ginkgoalean lineages had Ginkgo-like leaves but differently arranged reproductive structures from living and fossil Ginkgo.

title: First octopuses

facts.text: The earliest octopuses appeared in the Middle Jurassic, having split from the vampyromorphs in the Triassic to Early Jurassic.
Molecular evidence suggests the squid and octopus lineage split from the belemnoids in the Permian.
One timeline lists the oldest known octopus fossil at about 296 Ma.

title: Sundance Sea floods northwestern North America

facts.text: From the Middle Jurassic, the shallow Sundance Sea covered much of northwest North America in five successive marine transgressions.
Dinosaurs left tracks along its shores, as at Red Gulch in Wyoming.
It retreated for the last time late in the Jurassic, buried by Morrison Formation river sediments.

title: Terranes accrete to western North America

facts.text: The Alexander and Wrangellia terranes, long isolated in Panthalassa, were accreted to western North America in the Middle Jurassic.
The Cache Creek Ocean probably closed at the same time, and the Stikinia terrane was also added during the Jurassic.
The first terrane collisions on the western edge of North America came in the early Triassic, when the Quesnel, Cache Creek and Stikine terranes combined to form the Intermontane Superterrane.
The likely order of arrival was Yukon-Tanana, Quesnel, Cache Creek and Stikine, although it is also possible these terranes were assembled as one unit before reaching North America.

title: Theropods split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs

facts.text: By the Middle Jurassic, tetanuran theropods had reached every continent and split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs.
Allosauroids were the first giant theropods, over 2 tonnes; Asfaltovenator of South America may be the oldest.
Coelurosaurs first appeared too, including early tyrannosauroids such as Proceratosaurus from the Bathonian of Britain.

title: Sea level climbs from the Aalenian onward

facts.text: Sea level rose steadily from the Aalenian, apart from dips in the Bajocian and near the Callovian–Oxfordian boundary.
It peaked possibly 140 metres above today's at the Kimmeridgian–Tithonian boundary, probably because seafloor spreading sped up.
Sea level had fallen sharply in the Early Jurassic and stayed low through the Middle Jurassic before rising considerably toward the Late Jurassic, deepening seaways between continents.
Carnosaurs first appeared in the Middle Jurassic around 174 Ma; their last definite family, the carcharodontosaurids, died out about 90 Ma.
Distinctive characteristics of carnosaurs include large eye sockets, a long narrow skull, and a thigh bone (femur) longer than the shin (tibia).
The largest carnosaurs can reach up to 10 meters in length.
Most former carnosaurs, such as the megalosaurids, the spinosaurids and the ceratosaurs, were reclassified as more primitive theropods.

title: Middle Jurassic dinosaur sites of Skye

facts.text: Middle Jurassic rocks of Skye's Trotternish peninsula, about 174-166 million years old, preserve dinosaur footprints and bones.
Bones of large theropods, sauropods and thyreophorans have been found there, with footprints of all three at Staffin Bay, Duntulm and Brother's Point.
There is a paucity of dinosaur fossils from the Early and Middle Jurassic, but by the Late Jurassic dinosaurs were dominating the planet.

sources.title: 2.7: Phanerozoic Eon - Mesozoic Era - Geosciences LibreTexts (Historical Geology (Bentley et al.))

title: Middle Jurassic Cool Interval follows Toarcian warmth

facts.text: After the Toarcian Warm Interval ended around 174 Ma, the Middle Jurassic Cool Interval followed, lasting until about 164 Ma.
The cool interval may have been broken by brief icehouse episodes, including a possible short-lived ice age in the late Bajocian.
Europe turned noticeably more humid at the Aalenian–Bajocian boundary, then drier during the middle Bajocian.
The Callovian–Oxfordian boundary, at the close of the cool interval, saw especially marked global cooling, possibly even an ice age.

conflicts.note: Same page puts the end of the MJCI at the Callovian–Oxfordian boundary (161.5 Ma) rather than 164 Ma

facts.text: The earliest unequivocal stegosaurs, such as Adratiklit, Bashanosaurus and Thyreosaurus, come from the Bajocian–Bathonian.
Aalenian footprints from England (Deltapodus) are the oldest probable stegosaur record.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth and Timeline of life (de6ef705b189) list first stegosaurs at 176 Ma

facts.text: Cryptoclidid and elasmosaurid plesiosaurs first appeared around 170 Ma.
By about 160 Ma cryptoclidids, fairly short plesiosaurs with long necks and small heads, were present.
Elasmosaurids grew up to 15 m long, with as many as 76 neck vertebrae, more than any other known vertebrate.

conflicts.note: Plesiosaur page: the Elasmosauridae appeared later in the Early Cretaceous

facts.text: Megalosaurids, the oldest radiation of tetanuran theropods, first appeared in Europe during the Bajocian, around 170 Ma.
By the late Middle Jurassic, megalosaurines were already among the largest land predators.
The earliest members of the Tetanurae appeared during the late Early Jurassic or early Middle Jurassic.
The first salamanders and newts appeared around 170 Ma.
Early crown-group salamanders such as Chunerpeton and Pangerpeton are known from the Middle–Late Jurassic Yanliao Biota of China.
By the end of the Jurassic salamanders had reached North America, as Iridotriton from the Morrison Formation shows.

title: Central Atlantic widens into the Atlantic Gateway

facts.text: As Pangaea broke up between about 170 and 150 Ma, the young Atlantic Ocean began to form a seaway, the 'Atlantic Gateway'.
By the Late Jurassic a still-narrow Atlantic had just separated Europe from North America.
A rift spread from the spreading Central Atlantic along the continental margin of northwestern France toward Aquitaine.
The deep basins that later held the Paratethys formed in the Oxfordian as an extension of the Central Atlantic rift.

title: Weak geomagnetic field and the 'Jurassic Quiet Zone'

facts.text: Earth's magnetic field was weak from about 170 to 130 Ma, so the deep seafloor of that age carries faint magnetic anomalies.
These faint stripes, off eastern North America, northwest Africa and in the western Pacific, were once read as a 'Jurassic Quiet Zone' superchron, but rocks on land record reversals.
The oldest seafloor surviving today dates to about 170 Ma.
From 170 to 120 Ma Iberia slid more than 200 km sideways past Europe as it rifted away from the Grand Banks.
In the Late Jurassic the Iberian microcontinent broke from the European plate, and the Valais Ocean opened between them.
In the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic there were two stages of rifting, with extension and subsidence, on the western margin of Iberia.
In the Late Jurassic Africa started moving east and the Alpine Tethys opened.
An impact in what is now Poltava Oblast, Ukraine, left the Obolon' crater, a confirmed buried structure about 20 km across.
One estimate puts its age at 169 ± 7 million years, in the Middle Jurassic.

title: First unambiguous squamates

facts.text: The oldest unambiguous squamate fossils are Bathonian, from the Northern Hemisphere, when many modern groups, snakes included, first appear; a timeline dates the first lizards to about 168 Ma.
Crown squamates probably originated in the Early Jurassic: their last common ancestor is estimated at about 190 Ma, and one timeline puts the first squamates at about 199 Ma.
Squamates, the lizards and snakes, first diversified during the Jurassic and kept diversifying through the Cretaceous.
Snakes probably evolved from burrowing or aquatic lizards; their earliest fossils date to between 167 and 143 Ma.
By the Late Jurassic, early gecko relatives such as Eichstaettisaurus and the oldest accepted anguimorph, Dorsetisaurus, had appeared.

facts.text: The oldest unequivocal choristodere, the small lizard-like Cteniogenys, comes from Middle Jurassic (Bathonian) rocks in Britain, about 168–166 Ma.
Choristoderes were freshwater aquatic reptiles of uncertain affinity; the order lasted until the Miocene.
Coeruleodraco, from China's Late Jurassic, was a more advanced choristodere but still small and lizard-like.

conflicts.note: Jurassic page gives only the Middle Jurassic for the earliest choristoderes

facts.text: The earliest known multituberculates, such as Hahnotherium and Kermackodon, come from Middle Jurassic (Bathonian) rocks of England and Russia, about 168–166 Ma.
One of the most successful mammal orders, they survived and dominated for over 100 million years, longer than any other mammaliaform order, until the Oligocene.
In the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous, early multituberculates were abundant and widespread across Laurasia.

conflicts.note: Jurassic page and the Multituberculata lead (c9886d1d3605) give only the Middle Jurassic

facts.text: Fossils about 167 Ma old, including Ambondro, Amphilestes, Amphitherium and teeth from Madagascar, show the monotreme and therian lines had split, dating the crown group's appearance.
Other sources put the crown group's origin, from earlier mammaliaforms, in the Early Jurassic, probably late in that epoch.
Mammaliaforms, among the few cynodont lineages to survive the end-Triassic extinction, diversified extensively in the Jurassic; the docodont Castorocauda shows they already had fur.
Jurassic mammals stayed small, mostly under 10 kilograms, but spread widely; about 150 Ma the chipmunk-sized Fruitafossor seems to have dug into social-insect nests, probably termites'.
Cladotherian mammals first appeared around 170 Ma, and in the Late Jurassic dryolestidans were among the most diverse mammal groups in North America and Europe.

conflicts.note: Mammal § Origins, Therapsida (6ba4d9f23189) and Middle Jurassic ('late Early Jurassic', d5760f53fbd0) place the origin in the Early Jurassic

title: Turgai Sea divides Europe from Asia

facts.text: During the Callovian the Turgai Epicontinental Sea formed, a marine barrier between Europe and Asia.

title: Oxford Clay Sea and its marine reptiles

facts.text: The Oxford Clay, a marine mudstone of Callovian-Oxfordian age, settled over much of southeast England, from Dorset to Yorkshire.
Its sea held plesiosaurs such as Liopleurodon and Cryptoclidus, marine crocodiles, the ichthyosaur Ophthalmosaurus, belemnites and bivalves such as Gryphaea.
Its lower Peterborough Member is a fossil-rich organic mudstone, and at Christian Malford, Wiltshire, it preserves exceptionally detailed coleoid fossils.

facts.text: North America began separating from South America in the Early Jurassic, opening the gulf in a new rift beside what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.
Seafloor spreading in the Gulf of Mexico began about 165 Ma, in the Middle Jurassic.
The Maya Block was carried away from the Laurentian craton as the gulf opened and North America drifted northwest, away from Pangaea.
The Florida Platform, once part of Africa, stayed with North America and gathered carbonate, evaporite and siliciclastic sediments as the gulf opened.
How Middle America's crustal blocks moved after 170 Ma is still not widely agreed upon.

conflicts.note: Florida Platform, Suwannee terrane and Geological history of Earth place the gulf's opening in the Early Jurassic
Maya Block page (cites 2021) and Florida Platform (0ccd21fd8568) place the opening in the Middle Jurassic; consistent with, but less precise than, 165 Ma

facts.text: The Zapadnaya crater in Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine, about 3.2 km across, formed about 165 ± 5 million years ago, in the Middle Jurassic.

title: Mountain building begins in western North America

facts.text: Between 165 and 155 Ma an exotic terrane, the Mezcalera promontory, began to be subducted, and Rocky Mountain orogenesis began.
A volcanic flare-up in the Sierra Nevada arc ran from 170 to 150 Ma.
Deformation in the southern Sevier fold-and-thrust belt began around 160 Ma.
The Yanliao Biota, fossil beds of northeastern China spanning about 165 to 150 Ma, includes the Tiaojishan and Haifanggou formations.
Alternating volcanic tuff and sediment preserved some of the world's best Jurassic fossils: dinosaurs, mammals, salamanders, insects, lizards and plants.
The Daohugou beds formed between 164 and 158 Ma; the Tiaojishan Formation spans from 165 Ma to between 156 and 153 Ma.
The Haifanggou Formation adds fossil arthropods, amphibians, pterosaurs and mammaliaforms.
A warm phase, the Kimmeridgian Warm Interval, followed the Middle Jurassic cool spell and lasted from about 164 to 150 Ma.
Fossil wood suggests it was one of the wettest stretches of the Jurassic.
A widening Central Atlantic and western Indian Ocean supplied new moisture, softening seasonal swings in the Pangaean interior.
Very high carbon dioxide levels in the Late Jurassic drove high temperatures around the globe through the greenhouse effect.
Europe nonetheless grew steadily more arid over the Late Jurassic.
Pterodactyloid pterosaurs first appeared around 163 Ma.
Pterosaur diversity peaked in the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.
The Lhasa terrane began colliding with the Qiangtang terrane about 163–145 Ma, joining it along the Bangong suture; the collision lasted into the early Late Cretaceous.
Lhasa was one of the terranes, with West Burma, that rifted from northern Gondwana in the Triassic and Jurassic and later collided with Asia.
The sutured Lhasa terrane now forms southern Tibet.

conflicts.note: Himalayas page places the collision in the Early Cretaceous
Gondwana page (cites 2001): Lhasa collided with Asia in the Early Cretaceous

facts.text: The two living turtle groups, Pleurodira and Cryptodira, had diverged by the beginning of the Late Jurassic.
The oldest pleurodires, the Platychelyidae, and the oldest unambiguous cryptodire, Sinaspideretes from China, are Late Jurassic.
The Thalassochelydia, a diverse marine turtle lineage unrelated to modern sea turtles, lived in Late Jurassic Europe and South America.

title: Kimmeridge Clay, North Sea oil source rock

facts.text: Fossil-rich marine clay holding ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and pliosaurs built up from the Late Jurassic into the earliest Cretaceous, from Dorset to Lincolnshire and the North Sea.
Algae and bacteria buried in Jurassic seafloor mud became North Sea oil and gas; the Kimmeridge Clay and its equivalents are the province's major source rock.
Elsewhere, the Jurassic Sargelu and Naokelekan formations source Iraq's oil, and the Middle-Late Jurassic Arabian Intrashelf Basin holds the world's largest oil reserves.

conflicts.note: Ichthyosaur and plesiosaur tables date the clay's fauna to the Kimmeridgian

title: Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean closes

facts.text: After closing gradually from west to east since the Late Triassic, the ocean shut in a rapid scissor-like collision of Siberia with the North China–Amuria and Erguna blocks.
The closure raised the Verkhoyansk–Kolyma mountain belt of Siberia.
Paleomagnetic data suggest its oceanic crust subducted beneath Mongolia's terranes in the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous.

title: Sponge and coral reefs expand

facts.text: Reefs, which had declined at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, expanded greatly in the Late Jurassic, both sponge reefs and scleractinian coral reefs.
They resembled modern reefs but had more microbial carbonate and hypercalcified sponges, and weaker biological binding.
Crabs, rare until then, became abundant as they moved into reefs, whose crevices sheltered them from predators.

title: Teleost fishes begin a major diversification

facts.text: Teleosts, now over 99% of living ray-finned fish, began a major diversification in the Late Jurassic.
Early members of modern teleost groups such as Elopomorpha and Osteoglossoidei appeared at this time.
The earliest known ellimmichthyiforms, and clupeomorphs as a whole, come from the Late Jurassic of Peru.
The oldest anatomically modern gars also appeared in the Late Jurassic.

title: Tendaguru dinosaur beds of Tanzania

facts.text: The Tendaguru Beds of south-eastern Tanzania, a Lagerstätte known for large dinosaur bonebeds, are the richest Late Jurassic strata in Africa.
Its dinosaurs lived on semi-arid coastal plains in the subtropical south, alternating with shallow seas; the fauna resembles the Morrison Formation's and stayed stable through the Late Jurassic.
Finds include Giraffatitan, the tallest and heaviest dinosaur known from good skeletons, and over a thousand bones of the stegosaur Kentrosaurus.

title: Zuñi sequence transgression begins

facts.text: The Zuñi sequence, North America's major cratonic sequence after the Absaroka, began in the latest Jurassic, peaked in the Late Cretaceous and ended by the Paleocene.

facts.text: Ceratopsian dinosaurs appear in the fossil record around 161 Ma, represented by Yinlong.
These first ceratopsians, members of the Chaoyangsauridae, lived in Late Jurassic China.
The oldest known eutherian is the small, shrew-like Juramaia sinensis from China, dated to about 160 Ma.
Juramaia sits closer to the ancestry of placental mammals than to marsupials.

The earliest proposed placental mammal, Juramaia, is Jurassic, yet the earliest known monotreme, Teinolophus, is Cretaceous, even though placentals are more derived and should appear after monotremes.
Recalibrations of genetic and morphological diversity rates have suggested a Late Cretaceous origin for placentals and a Paleocene origin for most modern clades.

title: New ocean floor parts East and West Gondwana

facts.text: Around 160 Ma Africa separated from Antarctica; India followed in the Early Cretaceous.
East and West Gondwana parted, with new oceanic crust forming between them about 160–155 Ma.
Narrow ocean basins opened between Eastern Gondwana (Antarctica, Australia, India, Madagascar), Western Gondwana (Africa, Arabia, South America) and Laurasia.
East Antarctica moved south faster than Africa and South America, opening the Weddell, Riiser-Larsen, Mozambique and Somali basins; Weddell Sea spreading began about 147 Ma.
Australia and Antarctica began pulling apart in the Late Jurassic, and magmatism of the Australia–India breakup, 158–136 Ma, built the Wallaby Plateau.

conflicts.note: Cape Fold Belt dates Gondwana's break-up to about 150 Ma

facts.text: An impact made the Vepriai crater, 8 km across and Lithuania's largest.
Its age is estimated at more than 160 ± 10 million years, in the Middle or Late Jurassic.

title: Morrison Formation and its sauropod giants

facts.text: The Morrison Formation of western North America, mostly river and floodplain deposits, was laid down between about 156.3 and 146.8 Ma.
It accumulated as the Sundance Sea retreated before highlands rising to the west.
It holds one of the best-known sauropod faunas, 24 recognized species, among them Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Barosaurus, Camarasaurus and Diplodocus.
Predators such as Allosaurus, Ceratosaurus and Torvosaurus left bite marks on bones at the Mygatt-Moore Quarry.
Morrison quarries about 150 Ma old are dense with dinosaurs; at Cleveland-Lloyd, the densest known Jurassic concentration, animals died around a drought-stricken pond.

title: Argoland rifts from northwestern Australia

facts.text: A hypothetical landmass, Argoland, has been suggested to have rifted off northwestern Australia about 155 Ma.
A 2023 reconstruction treats it as an archipelago of microcontinental fragments, now in southwest Borneo and nearby, rather than one continent.

contested_note: Argoland is a hypothetical landmass; its form and where its remains lie are debated.

facts.text: Huayangosaurus, an early stegosaur, lived in China in the Bathonian, about 166 Ma; by the Callovian–Oxfordian, much larger stegosaurs such as Tuojiangosaurus followed.
Stegosaurids had their greatest radiation in the Late Jurassic; stegosaurs and theropods diversified around 155 Ma.
Stegosaurus itself is known from the Kimmeridgian upper Morrison Formation of Wyoming.
The Nevadan orogeny built mountains along western North America's margin from about 155 to 145 Ma; mountain building continued in the Cretaceous Sevier and Laramide orogenies.
The first of several massive batholiths were emplaced in the northern Cordillera from the mid-Jurassic, marking the Nevadan orogeny.
It began as an Andean-type magmatic arc while the Farallon plate subducted beneath North America.
Arc magmatism and the accretion of oceanic arcs built the ancestral Sierra Nevada and Klamath Mountains.
Terranes such as the Tuolumne River and Slate Creek were added to the continent, and the Josephine Ophiolite formed about 155–150 Ma.

conflicts.note: Geological history of Earth (cites 1997) starts the orogeny's batholiths in the mid-Jurassic

title: First pines and the pine family

facts.text: The oldest unambiguous member of the pine family is the cone Eathiestrobus from the Kimmeridgian of Scotland, the group's only certain pre-Cretaceous fossil.
The earliest pine trees are dated to about 153 Ma.
By the end of the Jurassic most modern conifer groups had appeared, descended from voltzialean ancestors.
Archaeopteryx, long considered the earliest bird though the avian–non-avian boundary is unclear, lived around 150 Ma in southern Germany, then a warm tropical archipelago.
Birds evolved from small predatory coelurosaurian theropods of the clade Paraves; the first stem-group birds appeared in the Jurassic, several sources say the Late Jurassic.
The earliest avialans appear in the Middle to Late Jurassic, definitively represented by Archaeopteryx.
Its fossils already carry advanced flight feathers, so feathers must have begun evolving before the Late Jurassic.
With lizards, birds are among the living reptile groups that first appeared in the Jurassic.

conflicts.note: Bird page; Timeline of Earth and Timeline of life also give c. 155 Ma (first birds)
Evolution of birds (cites 2016) and the Jurassic lead (f7b929f29a24) date the first birds only to the Jurassic as a whole

facts.text: About 150 Ma Cimmeria finally collided with Laurasia and stalled; the ocean floor behind it buckled under, forming the Tethys Trench.
Late Jurassic collisions of Cimmerian crustal fragments with Eurasia are recorded in Greece's Hellenic orogeny.
Cimmeria, a piece of shelf, traveled north over about 60 million years, pushing the floor of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean under the eastern end of northern Pangaea.
The Neo-Tethys Ocean formed between Cimmeria and Gondwana, directly over where the Paleo-Tethys had been.
The Jurassic closed with the Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval, which began about 150 Ma and lasted into the Early Cretaceous.
A marked temperature drop, the Early Tithonian Cooling Event, came during the Tithonian.
The Solnhofen limestones of Bavaria, a Tithonian Konservat-Lagerstätte about 149–148 Ma old, preserve fine imprints of soft-bodied animals such as jellyfish.
The area was an archipelago at the edge of the Tethys, with salty lagoons whose oxygen-free bottom waters kept scavengers away.
Animals and plants washed into the lagoons were buried in soft carbonate mud, preserving dragonfly wings and stray feathers.
Over 600 species are known, including 29 kinds of pterosaur and the famous early bird Archaeopteryx.
Nearby sites of the same Solnhofen Archipelago, such as Ettling, preserve fish, horseshoe crabs, beetles, crustaceans and turtles.

conflicts.note: Archaeopteryx page: early Tithonian Solnhofen limestone

facts.text: The Arctic Ocean opened from around 148 to 70 Ma, accompanied by the High Arctic Large Igneous Province.
Pangaea's breakup across the Jurassic–Cretaceous opened the Amerasian Basin and the Arctic Ocean.
As the Atlantic and Arctic oceans opened during the Mesozoic and into the Cenozoic, the Arctic Region went through several stages of rifting, sedimentation and magmatism.
The flood basalts in the Canadian Arctic Islands are similar to the Columbia River flood basalts of the Pacific Northwest.
An L-chondrite asteroid 5–10 km wide struck what is now South Africa's North West province, in the Tithonian about 146 Ma.
The buried structure's size is debated, from 75–80 km to 240 km; the latest estimate is about 190 km.
It struck several million years before the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.
An iridium layer in Tithonian rocks of Brazil's Araripe basin may be linked to it.

verification.title: Timescales of impact melt sheet crystallization and the precise age of the Morokweng impact structure, South Africa

facts.text: The Karoo large igneous province ended about 145 Ma with peripheral eruptions in Patagonia, the Antarctic Peninsula, northern South Africa, Kerala and southeast Australia.

title: Tamu Massif and Shatsky Rise erupt

facts.text: Lava erupted at the Pacific-Farallon-Izanagi triple junction in the northwest Pacific, building the Shatsky Rise, Earth's third-largest oceanic plateau.
Its oldest and largest edifice, Tamu Massif, formed in one brief eruptive period of a few million years and then became extinct.
Tamu's basalt dome spans about 450 by 650 km, comparable to New Mexico, with slopes of at most one degree.
It is likely the largest volcano yet found on Earth, though gaps in seismic profiles leave open whether it is one volcano or several.
Its origin is debated: a mantle plume, decompression melting at a mid-ocean ridge, or a recycled mantle slab.

conflicts.note: Tamu Massif geology section
Shatsky Rise: eruption of the whole LIP

verification.title: Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary age and mid-ocean-ridge–type mantle source for Shatsky Rise

title: End-Jurassic faunal turnover

facts.text: The end-Jurassic was once counted among eight mass extinctions; it is now seen as a complex turnover, some groups rising and others declining.
The evidence is mainly European, and the turnover was probably driven by sea level, which fell in the late Tithonian and rose again at the boundary.
Reefs declined sharply at the close of the Jurassic, cutting decapod crustacean diversity.
Most life was not strongly affected; several ichthyosaur and pliosaur lineages crossed the boundary.
The boundary, 143.1 ± 0.6 Ma on the ICS chart, is the only period boundary still lacking a GSSP.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether the end-Jurassic was a minor mass extinction or a milder, mostly European faunal turnover.
